summary: This standards-track document defines a TLV for the IS-IS routing protocol so routers can say they are using Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD). Without it, IS-IS may not react properly to a link failure that BFD detects in some situations. The TLV makes routers coordinate correctly.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers use a quick ping to notice a broken link. This adds a flag in their routing messages so neighbors know the quick ping is on and react when it fails.

questions: what is the is-is bfd-enabled tlv
why does is-is need a bfd tlv
subtitle: A flag in IS-IS hello packets that tells neighbors BFD is on, so a broken forwarding path is not missed.

tldr.problem: IS-IS hellos do not travel over IPv4 or IPv6, so a router can form an adjacency with a neighbor whose IP forwarding is broken and wrongly assume that the neighbor just does not support BFD.
tldr.mechanism: A router advertises a BFD-Enabled TLV (type 148) in its hellos, listing the topology and protocol pairs for which BFD is enabled. A neighbor then requires a working BFD session before treating the adjacency as usable.
tldr.outcome: IS-IS can react properly to every forwarding failure that BFD detects, including on startup or restart.

today: RFC 6213 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2011, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol, defined in RFC 5880, lets a router detect a forwarding plane failure between two routers. RFC 5882 describes using BFD to verify the forwarding ability of the adjacencies of an IS-IS router (IS-IS itself is in RFC 1195), but its method does not cover certain failure scenarios.

RFC 6213 defines a type-length-value (TLV) that allows a proper response to all forwarding failures when BFD is used with IS-IS.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD is a fast way for two routers to check that the road between them works. This RFC fixes a gap in how IS-IS uses that check.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
To allow mixed use, where some routers run BFD and some do not, RFC 5882 does not require a BFD session before an IS-IS adjacency is formed. If router A has neighbors B and C, and B does not support BFD, A still forms adjacencies with both and sets up a BFD session only with C.

This assumes that IS-IS Hellos (IIHs) share fate with forwarded data packets. That is not a fair assumption, because BFD mainly protects IPv4 and IPv6 forwarding while IS-IS does not use IPv4 or IPv6 to send or receive its hellos. If C has an IPv4 forwarding failure that still lets hellos through, then when A starts or restarts it will assume C simply lacks BFD, form an adjacency, and may incorrectly forward IPv4 traffic through C.
sections.plainLanguage: If the walkie-talkie is silent, you cannot tell whether your friend has none or whether their bridge is broken. The hellos still get through even when the real road is broken.

sections.title: The Solution: Advertise That BFD Is Enabled
sections.content:
An IS-IS router advertises that BFD is enabled on an interface by including a TLV in its IIHs. When sending an IIH on a BFD-enabled interface, a router that supports this extension MUST include the BFD-enabled TLV, listing the Multi-Topology Identifier (MTID) and Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID) pairs that have BFD enabled. On an interface where BFD is NOT enabled, it MUST NOT include the TLV.

The receiver tracks state for each neighbor with a set of variables:

  • ISIS_TOPO_NLPID_BFD_REQUIRED is TRUE for an MTID/NLPID pair when both the local system and the neighbor support BFD for it.
  • ISIS_TOPO_BFD_REQUIRED is the OR of those values for an MTID, and ISIS_BFD_REQUIRED is the AND of the per-topology values.
  • ISIS_TOPO_NLPID_STATE follows the BFD session state when BFD is required, and is otherwise TRUE.
  • ISIS_TOPO_USEABLE is the AND of the states for a topology, and ISIS_NEIGHBOR_USEABLE is the OR of all topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router puts up a sign saying what it checks with BFD. The neighbor keeps a scoreboard of which roads are both promised and confirmed working.

sections.title: Adjacency Rules and Transitions
sections.content:
Whenever ISIS_BFD_REQUIRED is TRUE, these rules MUST apply. ISIS_NEIGHBOR_USEABLE MUST be TRUE before an adjacency moves from INIT to UP, and if it becomes FALSE while the adjacency is UP, the adjacency MUST go DOWN. On a point-to-point circuit the Three-Way adjacency state is set to DOWN in the Three-Way Adjacency TLV of RFC 5303 while it is FALSE. On a LAN circuit the IS Neighbors TLV with the neighbor's MAC address MUST be omitted. A topology-specific neighbor is advertised only when ISIS_TOPO_USEABLE is TRUE for that topology.

For a non-disruptive transition, some time should be allowed before bringing down an UP adjacency when a neighbor's TLV newly requires BFD. A simple way is to not update the adjacency hold time on such hellos until ISIS_NEIGHBOR_USEABLE becomes TRUE. If a BFD session is administratively shut down, IS-IS SHOULD allow time for the MTID/NLPID to be removed from the neighbor's TLV, again by not updating the hold time.
sections.plainLanguage: A road only counts as open when the walkie-talkie check works. If a friend newly says they are using one, you give them a little time to get it working before you close the road.

sections.title: The BFD-Enabled TLV Format
sections.content: The TLV has type 148. Its length is the number of octets in the value field, from 3 to 255. The value holds 3 octets for each topology and data protocol with BFD enabled: 2 octets with four reserved bits and the MTID, then 1 octet with the NLPID, as defined in ISO 9577. The TLV SHALL only be included in an IIH, and only when BFD is enabled for one or more supported MTID/protocols on the sending interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign is a list. Each entry is three small pieces of information saying which road and which kind of traffic is being checked.

sections.title: Graceful Restart, Security and IANA
sections.content:
When IS-IS graceful restart (RFC 5306) and BFD are used together and BFD shares fate with the control plane, a BFD failure can coincide with a restart. Aborting graceful restart because of it is undesirable, so ignoring the BFD failure for a limited time would be beneficial. How to do this is outside the scope of the document.

Misusing the TLV could prevent an adjacency from forming or cause bidirectional forwarding failures to go undetected, both forms of denial of service. However, a party that can manipulate the TLV can already disrupt IS-IS in other ways. The TLV does not change the use of authentication by IS-IS or BFD. IANA registered TLV type 148 for IIH only (not LSP, SNP or purge).
sections.plainLanguage: If a router is restarting, a failed check might just be the restart, so it is smart to be patient. Someone who could mess with the sign could already cause trouble in other ways.
